How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

The Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition (WPPSI-IV), is widely used to assess young children's cognitive abilities. Its indices describe performance in domains such as verbal comprehension and working memory, but evidence for interpreting these as distinct abilities remains limited. This study examined whether exploratory graph analysis (EGA), a network method, could recover the proposed index groupings from published normative correlations for ages 2:6 to 3:11 (n = 600) and 4:0 to 7:7 (n = 1,100). Simulations tested whether the same method could recover those groupings when separate, correlated factors generated the data. The main EGA procedure placed the primary subtests in one group. It also produced one group in 99.6% to 100% of samples generated from the index models, so it could not distinguish those models from simpler alternatives. In the older band, however, factor models fit better with several factors than with one. Recovery depended on factor correlations, the number of subtests per factor, and a built-in check for a single dimension. Groupings also changed with subtest coverage. For school psychologists, a one-group network result, however consistent, cannot by itself show whether WPPSI-IV index scores reflect distinct abilities.

Introduction

The Wechsler scales are among the most widely used cognitive assessments in school psychology, both in the United States and internationally (Benson et al., 2019; Oakland et al., 2016). Interpreting patterns among their index scores is taught in cognitive assessment courses (Lockwood & Farmer, 2020; Miller et al., 2021). Widely used texts reinforce this practice. The current edition of Sattler's assessment text connects intelligence theory with Wechsler interpretation and report writing (Sattler, 2024). Other sources use cognitive and neuropsychological frameworks to link test results to explanations of a child's learning difficulties and to recommendations for diagnosis and intervention (Flanagan et al., 2022; Kaufman et al., 2016). Within these frameworks, index scores become part of an account of how a child thinks and learns. Proponents of patterns of strengths and weaknesses (PSW) methods use cognitive profiles to help identify learning disabilities (Schneider et al., 2024), and Wechsler profiles have been proposed as markers of ADHD and autism (see Wilson, 2024).

Several syntheses have not supported these diagnostic uses. A systematic review concluded that PSW methods identify learning disabilities at the level of chance, regardless of method or instrument (Dombrowski, Benson, et al., 2025). Across 19 meta-analyses, the estimated overlap between students with and without learning disabilities exceeded 50% on cognitive measures (Burns et al., 2025). A meta-analysis of the WAIS-IV and WISC-V found that people with ADHD scored mostly at age-expected levels and that Wechsler profiles were not sensitive or specific enough for diagnosis (Wilson, 2024). When a school psychologist describes an index difference as a distinct cognitive weakness, that interpretation can shape the explanation given to a family and the recommendations made to an educational team.

These uses also assume that each index measures a distinct ability. The Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition (WPPSI-IV; Wechsler, 2012), reports three primary indices for children aged 2:6 to 3:11 and five for children aged 4:0 to 7:7, each based on two subtests. Interpreting one of these scores as a cognitive strength or weakness therefore treats performance on two tasks as evidence of a broader ability. This study asks whether network analysis can distinguish the domains those indices are meant to measure.

Structural Evidence for Wechsler Indices

Reviews of profile interpretation also point to a structural problem (Farmer et al., 2021; McGill et al., 2018; Watkins, 2000). Structural research addresses part of the problem by asking whether the proposed domains can be distinguished and how much reliable information their scores provide beyond general ability. Because subtests share variance across domains, a domain score also reflects general ability (Brunner et al., 2012; Reise, 2012). A statistical model can separate domains even when their scores carry little reliable information unique to those domains (Gignac & Watkins, 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2016). WPPSI-IV factor analyses have distinguished domains whose scores contain little reliable information of their own. Watkins and Beaujean (2014), analyzing the same published correlations used here, found that general ability accounted for most of the shared variation among subtests. General-factor omega hierarchical was .78 in the younger band and .86 in the older band, and the older general factor accounted for 70.3% of common variance. Specificfactor coefficients were .20 for Verbal Comprehension, .08 for Visual Spatial, and .09 for Working Memory in the younger model and ranged from .05 to .33 in the older model, including .11 for Working Memory and .05 for Fluid Reasoning. These estimates describe modeled domain scores, including secondary subtests and two verbal specific factors in the older model. They do not estimate the reliability of differences between published index scores.

Even the number of domains can depend on the models and subtests examined. Studies of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition (WISC-V), challenged its five-groupfactor structure using the full U.S. standardization battery (Canivez et al., 2017 (Canivez et al., , 2018)). Primarybattery analyses supported four factors at ages 6-14 and five at ages 15-16 (Dombrowski et al., 2018). A clinical study using separate exploratory and confirmatory subsamples supported four group factors with a dominant general factor (Canivez et al., 2020). Several normative studies reanalyzed the same sample, so their agreement reflects comparisons among methods rather than independent replications. Other analyses support five domains. Dombrowski, McGill, et al. (2025) used Bayesian structural equation modeling of the 10 primary WISC-V subtests in 710 clinical cases. Their five-domain model included a higher-order general factor and a residual association between Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning. They reported simple structure and favored interpreting the indices beyond Full Scale IQ, while emphasizing general ability. Exploratory analyses of the same subtest configuration in 5,359 clinical cases drawn from the same clinic supported four factors (Dombrowski et al., 2022). The primary subtests have thus supported competing structural and interpretive conclusions across these studies.

Network Analysis and Recovery

Network analysis offers another way to evaluate the proposed groupings. Exploratory graph analysis (EGA) identifies communities, or groups of connected subtests, within a network of their statistical associations (Golino & Epskamp, 2017). In the networks used here, connections are partial correlations that account for the other included subtests (Epskamp & Fried, 2018). A partition specifies which subtests belong to each community. Watkins et al. (2023) analyzed the 10 primary WISC-V subtests in 7,149 clinical cases with 10,000 bootstrap samples. Their four-community solution combined visual-spatial and fluid-reasoning tasks, with 100% structural consistency for each community and 100% item stability. These measures describe the stability of the observed solution. Recovery addresses a different question: whether the procedure reproduces the structure used to generate simulated data (Christensen & Golino, 2021). A procedure can consistently combine subtests assigned to separate generating factors. Dombrowski et al. (2021) simulated data from normative correlations to compare rival factor models. Generating data from each fitted model extends that approach by giving the procedure a known structure to recover.

Earlier EGA simulations examined two indicators per factor, but not at the factor correlations estimated for the WPPSI-IV. Golino et al. (2020) used 3, 4, or 8 indicators in their multidimensional conditions, with interfactor correlations through .70, and accuracy declined as correlations increased. Golino and Demetriou (2017) reanalyzed simulated data with 2 to 10 indicators for each of six factors correlated .70 (Keith et al., 2016) and recovered six factors regardless of the number of indicators. Both studies assessed how many dimensions EGA returned rather than which subtests it grouped together, and both used earlier versions of the procedure. The present controlled grid adds factor correlations of .80 and .90 and assesses exact recovery of each subtest's grouping under the current procedure. It uses equal loadings and no cross-loadings, a simpler structure than the heterogeneous loadings and cross-loadings in the Golino et al. (2020) design. Recovery research also compares unidimensionality checks and community algorithms, making the analysis procedure another condition to examine (Christensen, 2024; Christensen et al., 2024). Rapuc et al. (2024) used WPPSI-IV networks to compare connectivity and centrality in very preterm and full-term French children. Their study did not ask whether network communities reproduce the proposed index groupings, and their published matrices, derived from estimated networks, could not be reanalyzed here. Subtest coverage also complicates interpretation of network findings. Lecerf et al. (2023) found three or four dimensions and substantial instability across five French WISC-V standardization age groups; final threedimensional solutions followed removal of unstable subtests. Dombrowski et al. (2026) found four communities in simulated data from the full 16-subtest U.S. WISC-V normative matrix.

Because these analyses used different sets of subtests, their results do not show how the smaller primary batteries are organized.

The Present Study

This study asked whether EGA could recover the WPPSI-IV primary-index groupings when those groupings were known to be present, and whether it could distinguish them from simpler structures. It extends network research on the WISC-V (Dombrowski et al., 2026; Watkins et al., 2023) to the WPPSI-IV and pairs the network analysis with recovery simulations based on models fitted to the normative correlations. Four research questions guided the analyses: 1.

What communities does EGA return for the WPPSI-IV subtests in each age band, and how stable are they across bootstrap samples? 2. Can EGA recover a known structure, including the WPPSI-IV index model, and under what measurement conditions does recovery succeed? 3. Are the communities similar across age bands when the subtests are held constant, and do they change when different subtests are analyzed within a band? 4. Do factor models fitted to the same normative correlations distinguish the index model from the merged and one-factor models?

Answering the third question required separating age from subtest coverage. The full younger and older batteries differ in both. Age-band analyses therefore used the seven shared subtests to hold the task set constant. Paired simulations compared nested configurations within the same generated samples to isolate the effect of changing coverage.

Method Normative Data

Analyses used published correlations from the WPPSI-IV Technical and Interpretive Manual (Wechsler, 2012, Table 5.1). The younger band covers ages 2:6 to 3:11 and contains 7 subtests; the older band covers ages 4:0 to 7:7 and contains 15. Band sample sizes of 600 and 1,100 were taken from Watkins and Beaujean (2014), who analyzed the same manual tables. The normative sample was stratified by age, sex, race/ethnicity, parent education level, and geographic region to match 2010 U.S. Census proportions (Wechsler, 2012). Individual normative records were unavailable. The correlations were transcribed twice from photographs of the manual, with no discrepancies among the 126 distinct off-diagonal coefficients. Both matrices were symmetric and positive definite.

Subtest Configurations

Six subtest configurations were analyzed. The younger-band full battery contains Information, Receptive Vocabulary, Picture Naming, Block Design, Object Assembly, Picture Memory, and Zoo Locations. The younger-band primary subtests omit Picture Naming, leaving the three primary index pairs. The older-band full battery contains all 15 older-band subtests. The older-band primary subtests are Information and Similarities, Block Design and Object Assembly, Matrix Reasoning and Picture Concepts, Picture Memory and Zoo Locations, and Bug Search and Cancellation. These pairs represent Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed, respectively.

The shared subtests are the seven subtests given in both age bands, analyzed in the same order in each band. In the younger band, the shared subtests are identical to the full battery, so the six configurations represent five distinct matrices derived from two normative sources. The full batteries describe the larger sets of subtests, the primary subtests address the index groupings, and the shared subtests permit age-band comparisons using matched tasks.

EGA Procedures

The main EGA procedure used the graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (GLASSO) to estimate a Gaussian graphical model (Friedman et al., 2008). The extended Bayesian information criterion selected regularization with γ = .50, 100 regularization values, and a minimum-to-maximum regularization ratio of .10 (Foygel & Drton, 2010).

Walktrap detected network communities (Pons & Latapy, 2006), and a Louvain check assessed unidimensionality from the empirical correlation matrix (Blondel et al., 2008; Christensen, 2024). GLASSO, Walktrap, and Louvain are EGAnet 2.4.1's default estimator, community algorithm, and unidimensionality method, respectively.

The Louvain unidimensionality check assesses whether the empirical correlation matrix yields a single community. If so, that one-community solution determines the reported dimensionality; otherwise, the estimated network's community solution is retained. The main sensitivity analysis omitted this check while keeping the GLASSO and Walktrap settings.

Additional sensitivities used leading-eigenvector and matrix-expansion checks, EBIC γ = .25, and Louvain community detection (Christensen et al., 2024; Golino et al., 2020).

Analyses used EGAnet 2.4.1 (Golino & Christensen, 2026), lavaan 0.6-17 (Rosseel, 2012), and R 4.3.3 (R Core Team, 2024), with igraph 1.6.0 and MASS 7.3-60.0.1 (Csárdi & Nepusz, 2006; Venables & Ripley, 2002). The master seed was 20260920, with stage-specific offsets. Scripts and session information are available in the online repository (see Data and Code Availability).

Bootstrap Stability and Configuration Comparisons

Parametric bootstrap EGA generated 1,000 multivariate normal samples per configuration from its published correlation matrix at the corresponding band sample size (Christensen & Golino, 2021). Outcomes included community-count frequencies, communityspecific structural consistency, median item stability, and selected pairwise co-assignment proportions. Structural consistency is the proportion of bootstrap samples in which all subtests with available assignments from an observed community retain its assignment after community labels are matched. Item stability is the corresponding proportion for each subtest; co-assignment is how often two subtests appear in the same community. Exact recurrence of the publisher's index partition was checked separately in the saved primary memberships.

The bootstrap without the check used independently generated samples and its own seeds. Percentages exclude unusable partitions. Count summaries for the main EGA procedure retain one replicate with an isolated node in each of the older-band full battery and primary subtests; pairwise co-assignment uses available memberships. Table 1 identifies the denominators. The younger-band full battery and shared subtests were simulated separately despite their identical matrices, allowing their Monte Carlo percentages to differ.

Paired simulations generated 1,000 full-battery samples per band and analyzed nested subsets within each sample. Agreement between assignments was measured with the adjusted Rand index (ARI), which adjusts for chance (Hubert & Arabie, 1985). ARI equals 1 for identical partitions and 0 for chance-level agreement; negative values indicate agreement below chance.

Full-battery memberships were restricted to the retained subtests before comparison. The ageband comparison used independent draws from the two normative matrices.

Fitted Models and Calibrated Recovery

Three models were fitted to each primary correlation matrix by maximum likelihood in lavaan, with standardized latent variables and no post hoc modification. The index model specified three correlated factors in the younger band and five in the older, using the primarysubtest allocations. The younger merged model separated Information and Receptive Vocabulary from the four visual-spatial and memory subtests. The older merged model contained a verbal factor, a six-subtest visual-fluid-memory factor, and a processing-speed factor. Its six-subtest factor included Zoo Locations, unlike the partition observed for the older-band primary subtests without the check. The merged models were candidate structures informed by the network results, and their subtest allocations were held fixed during fitting. Each band also included a one-factor model.

Fit comparisons used χ², degrees of freedom, comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) with its 90% confidence interval, standardized root mean square residual (SRMR), and Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Conventional guidelines informed the fit descriptions (Hu & Bentler, 1999). Models were retained as specified to avoid selecting modifications for better fit to the same data (MacCallum et al., 1992). All converged without reported improper solutions or warnings. Each model's implied correlation matrix served as a fixed generating population for 1,000 samples at the observed band sample size. Both EGA procedures were applied. Mean simulated correlations differed from their generating correlations by at most .0034. Outcomes included the frequency of one community, recovery of the generating count, and exact partition recovery.

Count recovery requires the correct number of groups. Exact recovery also requires the correct assignment of every subtest, allowing for arbitrary community labels, and was defined by ARI = 1.00 and the correct count. More than one community under a one-factor model counted as a false split.

Frequencies matching the observed primary partitions were also summarized descriptively. These frequencies concern the empirical partition, which may differ from the generating model's subtest allocation. Table 2 reports generating-model recovery and count distributions. Calibration covered the primary subtests only.

Controlled Simulations

The controlled design crossed indicators per factor (m = 2, 3, 4, or 5), interfactor correlation (ρ = .50, .60, .70, .80, or .90), standardized loading (λ = .60, .70, or .80), sample size (N = 300, 600, 1,100, or 2,000), and dimensionality (D = 3 or 5). Each of the 480 cells contained 500 replicates, yielding 240,000 generated data sets. Loadings were equal within cells, crossloadings were absent, and data were multivariate normal. Outcomes included exact partition and dimensionality recovery, ARI, one-community frequency, and failure to return a usable partition.

Failures were excluded from recovery denominators and reported separately: 0.95% for the main EGA procedure and 1.45% without the check. Marginal summaries pooled usable replicates across the other manipulated conditions. Cells with five indicators, ρ ≤ .70, and λ = .80 served as favorable reference conditions. Figures 1 and 2 summarize the design; complete condition-specific results are available in the online repository (see Data and Code Availability).

A later set of one-factor simulations crossed total indicators (p = 6, 10, 15, or 20), the three loading levels, and the four sample sizes. Its 48 cells contained 500 replicates each, for 24,000 data sets. Both procedures were applied to estimate false splitting. Results distinguish rates rounded to zero from observed zero counts. Reported summaries were checked by recomputation from saved output.

Results

Observed Communities and Bootstrap Stability

The main EGA procedure returned one community for every configuration except the older-band full battery (Table 1). The older-band full battery returned three: six verbal subtests; Block Design, Object Assembly, Matrix Reasoning, Picture Concepts, Picture Memory, and Zoo Locations; and three processing-speed subtests. Without the check, the shared subtests separated verbal from nonverbal tasks in both bands. The younger-band primary subtests still returned one community, and the older-band full battery retained its three-community partition. In the olderband primary subtests, the procedure grouped Information with Similarities; combined five visual, reasoning, and memory tasks; and grouped Zoo Locations with Bug Search and Cancellation. In neither band were the primary subtests grouped by index. Working Memory formed no separate community in the examined point solutions.

With the check, one community recurred in 100% of younger-band bootstrap replicates, 99.8% for the older-band primary subtests, and 99.9% for the older-band shared subtests. The older-band full battery returned three communities in 85.0% and two in 15.0%. Its communityspecific structural consistency values were .96, .83, and .85, with median item stability of .998.

Without the check, the observed count recurred in 54.6% of replicates for the younger-band primary subtests and 53.4% for the older-band primary subtests, compared with 87.5% for the older-band full battery and 99.8% for the older-band shared subtests. The younger index partition appeared in 12 of 999 usable primary replicates without the check; the older index partition appeared in none of 997.

Subtests from different indices were often grouped together. Under the main EGA procedure, proportions for selected pairs ranged from .90 to 1.00. Without the check, Picture Memory in the older-band primary subtests was grouped with Zoo Locations in 75.7% of replicates and with Block Design in 77.5%. Leading-eigenvector and expansion checks retained the counts from the main EGA procedure except that expansion returned two for the older-band shared subtests. EBIC γ = .25 and Louvain community detection did not change the counts.

Recovery Under Fitted Models

The main EGA procedure returned one community in 100% of younger-band replicates under every fitted model (Table 2). In the older band, one community occurred in 99.6% under both index and merged models and in 100% under the one-factor model. Exact index recovery occurred in 0 of 1,000 replicates in each band. Exact merged-model recovery was 0 of 1,000 in the younger band and 0.2% in the older.

Without the check, the older index model produced three communities in 62.0% of replicates, two in 31.0%, and four in 6.9%; no usable replicate returned five. Exact index recovery was 11 of 999 usable replicates in the younger band (1.1%) and 0 of 998 in the older.

Exact recovery of the merged partition was 15.7% and 76.3%, respectively. Under one-factor models, false splitting occurred in 4.3% of younger-band and 25.5% of older-band replicates.

The partition observed without the check for the older-band primary subtests was reproduced in 1.5% of replicates under the index model, 0.2% under the merged model, and 0 of 999 under the one-factor model. These descriptive frequencies concern that empirical partition, rather than recovery of each generating partition. No decision rule was evaluated for selecting a factor model from these frequencies.

Recovery Across the Controlled Design

Recovery under the main EGA procedure fell sharply as factor correlations increased, especially with two indicators per factor (Figure 1). Exact recovery with two indicators was .565 at ρ = .50, .031 at .60, and .001 at .70. No usable replicate recovered the partition at .80 or .90.

With five indicators, recovery reached .794 at .80. At .90, no replicate recovered the partition in any cell. The favorable reference cells, with five indicators, ρ ≤ .70, and λ = .80, recovered it in every replicate. In the selected 16 cells with two indicators, ρ = .80 or .90, λ = .70 or .80, and N = 600 or 1,100, the main EGA procedure recovered none of 8,000 generating partitions.

With two indicators, the main EGA procedure returned one community in 14.4% of replicates at ρ = .50, 86.1% at .60, and 98.8% at .70. Rates reached 99.9% to 100% at .80 and .90. Increasing sample size did not consistently improve recovery. At two indicators and ρ = .60, exact recovery declined from .088 at N = 300 to .002 at N = 2,000 (Figure 2A). At ρ = .80, pooled across indicator counts, rates were .205, .226, .227, and .221 across increasing sample sizes.

Without the check, exact recovery with two indicators was .667, .506, .360, .193, and .013 at correlations of .50 through .90. At ρ = .80, recovery increased from .480 at N = 300 to .804 at N = 2,000 across indicator counts; within the two-indicator condition it increased from .077 to .314 (Figure 2B). With two indicators and ρ = .50, increasing λ from .60 to .80 raised recovery from .465 to .908. Across the full design, recovery was lower with five factors than with three, .637 versus .798.

In the one-factor simulations, the main EGA procedure produced two false splits across 24,000 replicates, both at N = 300 with λ = .60 and at least 15 indicators. Without the check, false splitting averaged .190 and declined from .305 at N = 300 to .112 at N = 2,000. For 15 and 20 indicators, rates remained between .17 and .23 at N = 2,000, pooled across loadings. For six indicators, no false split occurred in 1,500 usable replicates at that sample size. No failures occurred with the check (0 of 24,000); the failure rate without the check was 0.36%.

Task Coverage

The shared subtests were grouped identically in both age bands: one community with the check and the same verbal-nonverbal partition without it (ARI = 1.00; Table 3). Without the check, two communities recurred in 74.3% of younger-band and 99.8% of older-band bootstrap replicates.

In the paired simulations, the older-band full battery returned three communities in 87.1% of replicates. Restricting the same samples to the primary subtests produced one community in 100% with the check. Without it, the primary subset returned three communities in 50.7% and two in 44.8%, and matched the full-battery grouping only partly (mean ARI = .52). Restricting to the seven shared subtests yielded one community in 100% with the check and two in 99.8% without it. In the younger band, removing Picture Naming changed the result without the check from two communities in 77.8% of replicates to one in 53.8% and two in 45.3%.

Factor Model Fit

All younger factor models had favorable approximate fit (Table 4). The index model yielded χ² = 2.9 with six degrees of freedom, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000, and SRMR = .009.

Its factor correlations ranged from .84 to .85. BIC values were 9412.5, 9406.5, and 9412.4 for the one-factor, merged, and index models, respectively.

In the older band, the one-factor model fit less well than either multifactor model. CFI was .923, .980, and .991 for the one-factor, merged, and index models; corresponding RMSEA values were .085, .045, and .034. The index model had better approximate fit. BIC provided little separation between the merged and index models, 27867.3 versus 27868.7, respectively. Older index-model factor correlations ranged from .60 to .87. Visual Spatial correlated .87 with Fluid Reasoning and .81 with Working Memory, and Fluid Reasoning correlated .86 with Working Memory.

Discussion

The main EGA procedure consistently grouped the WPPSI-IV primary subtests together, but the recovery simulations showed why that result did not settle their structure. It returned a single community in 100% of younger-band samples and 99.6% of older-band samples generated from the index models, nearly matching its behavior under the merged and one-factor models. A stable one-community result therefore provided little basis for choosing among these competing accounts of the primary indices. Factor models fitted to the same correlations offered a separate comparison, and in the older band they fit better with several factors than with one.

Stability and Recovery

The present study adds recovery simulations to the questions addressed by earlier WISC-V network studies. Watkins et al. (2023) found four highly stable communities among the 10 primary WISC-V subtests, with the visual-spatial and fluid-reasoning subtests combined. They used GLASSO and Walktrap in EGAnet 1.2.3 and assessed how consistently subtests were assigned to communities. Dombrowski et al. (2026) found four communities in the full 16subtest WISC-V, combining Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning while keeping Working Memory separate, and assessed the stability of subtest strength centrality and the precision of network connections (Epskamp et al., 2018). These analyses address how stable a network estimate is. Recovery simulations address whether a procedure can distinguish the structures it is being used to evaluate.

The two questions can have different answers. In the present study, the one-community solutions for the primary subtests recurred in 99.8% to 100% of bootstrap samples, yet the procedure returned one community in 99.6% to 100% of samples generated from the index models. A highly stable solution therefore did not show that the index structure was absent.

Whether the same limits apply to the WISC-V would require WISC-V calibration.

Conditions for Recovery

The unidimensionality check helps explain why the procedure so often combined the subtests. When the check finds a single community, that answer replaces the network's community solution. In the controlled one-factor simulations, it nearly eliminated false splitting: 2 false splits occurred in 24,000 samples, compared with an average rate of .190 without the check. Yet the same check suppressed distinctions specified in multidimensional generating models.

In the fitted-model simulations, dropping the check improved recovery of the broader merged groupings but still almost never recovered the indices themselves. For the older-band primary subtests, the procedure without the check returned three communities, yet it recovered the index partition in 0 of 998 samples generated from the index model. Several communities therefore did not mean the intended distinctions had been recovered. Without the check, the procedure also split one-factor data in 4.3% of younger-band and 25.5% of older-band samples.

Recovery depended jointly on indicator count and factor correlations. With two indicators, exact recovery under the main EGA procedure fell from .565 at a factor correlation of .50 to .001 at .70; no usable sample recovered the groupings at .80 or .90. The fitted WPPSI-IV models contained similarly high correlations: .84 to .85 among the younger factors, and .81 to .87 among Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, and Working Memory in the older band. These conditions help explain the difficulty of recovery. The grid's equal loadings and uniform correlations, however, do not reproduce the heterogeneous fitted models exactly. Golino and Demetriou (2017) recovered the number of factors with two indicators per factor correlated .70, whereas the main EGA procedure here almost never recovered even the number of factors under that condition. The two designs differed in the number of factors, loadings, and procedure version, and the present results do not show which difference accounts for the contrast.

Larger samples did not consistently improve recovery under the main EGA procedure; with two indicators per factor and a factor correlation of .60, its recovery fell from .088 at N = 300 to .002 at N = 2,000. Without the check, larger samples improved recovery in some conditions. The benefit of additional observations therefore depended on the procedure as well as the measurement conditions.

Task Coverage and Age Bands

The paired comparisons showed directly why the task set matters. The full older battery produced three communities in 87.1% of paired samples, while its 10 primary subtests produced one community every time with the check. In the younger band, dropping Picture Naming shifted the result without the check from two communities in 77.8% of samples to a near-even split between one and two. Dombrowski et al. (2022) argued for examining the WISC-V primary battery separately, and McGrew et al. (2023) tested whether their network conclusions about Woodcock-Johnson IV domains held under different selections of measures. Here, comparisons within the same generated samples showed that full-battery findings did not automatically carry over to the primary indices. A school psychologist reading a full-battery network study therefore cannot assume that its groupings describe the primary index scores reported for a child.

The same coverage issue affects comparisons between age bands. Restricting both WPPSI-IV analyses to the same seven subtests produced identical groupings with different bootstrap stability. Full-battery differences therefore cannot be attributed to age alone. These comparisons did not test longitudinal change or measurement invariance across ages.

Factor Model Fit

Factor models fitted to the same normative correlations did not support a one-factor account of the older-band primary subtests. In the older band, both multifactor models fit better than a one-factor model (CFI .980 and .991 versus .923). The index model had better approximate fit than the merged model, although BIC did not clearly separate them. All three younger-band models fit well, although BIC favored the merged model. The observed onecommunity solution did not establish a one-factor account of either age band. Dombrowski, McGill, et al. (2025) likewise found that a multidimensional model fit the WISC-V primary subtests and favored interpreting the indices beyond Full Scale IQ. Model fit of this kind supports a structure; it does not establish the accuracy of an individual child's profile.

Implications for School Psychologists

A child may perform relatively poorly on Picture Memory and Zoo Locations and also struggle to follow classroom instructions. The WPPSI-IV Working Memory Index summarizes performance on those two test tasks (Wechsler, 2012). A school psychologist who attributes the classroom difficulty to a working-memory weakness adds a causal explanation that the score alone cannot establish. Across a broader executive-function literature, performance-based measures correlate weakly with ratings of everyday executive functioning (median r = .19; Toplak et al., 2013), and WAIS-IV and WISC-V profiles have not proved sensitive or specific enough to diagnose ADHD (Wilson, 2024). Reviews of profile interpretation have also questioned the educational usefulness of such inferences (Farmer et al., 2021; McGill et al., 2018).

Score reliability and the accuracy of profile differences pose separate problems for such interpretations. Watkins and Beaujean (2014) found little reliable variance specific to modeled WPPSI-IV domains after accounting for general ability; their coefficients do not directly assess index-score differences. De Jong (2023) examined discrepancies between index scores and overall performance in the Dutch WISC-V and found that only 40% to 74% were accompanied by a discrepancy on the corresponding broad factor. Clinical guidance recommends considering scores alongside history, behavior, and other assessment information (Kaufman et al., 2016). Agreement among sources does not establish a cognitive cause or show that a profile-based intervention will help (McGill et al., 2018). A report can describe memory-task performance and classroom difficulty separately, then identify the evidence for any proposed connection. Intervention recommendations require evidence of benefit for the observed difficulty, which neither factor-model fit nor network stability supplies.

Limitations

The analyses used published, rounded correlations, so individual score distributions could not be examined. Simulations assumed multivariate normality and held fitted values fixed.

Because the models were fitted to the same correlations being analyzed, recovery results depend on those approximations. They neither incorporate parameter uncertainty nor independently confirm population structure.

The controlled simulation used equal loadings, uniform factor correlations, and no crossloadings. The fitted WPPSI-IV models are less uniform. Summary rates pool usable samples across conditions with different recovery rates and exclude samples in which the procedure failed to return a usable result. The one-factor simulations were added after the main results had been analyzed and interpreted.

Recovery simulations compared the main EGA procedure with the version omitting its unidimensionality check. Other estimation, community-detection, and factor-retention methods were not compared on those data. Recovery was tested only for the primary subtests, leaving the full older battery's three-community result untested. No independent clinical WPPSI-IV sample or measure of diagnostic accuracy, intervention benefit, or child functioning was analyzed.

Conclusion

The main EGA procedure grouped the WPPSI-IV primary subtests together, but it did the same when the simulated data contained separate correlated factors. Its result therefore cannot show whether the indices capture distinct parts of a young child's developing cognitive abilities, and it changed when different subtests were analyzed. In the older band, factor models fit better with several factors than with one, and the index model had better approximate fit than the merged model, but BIC barely separated the two. In the younger band, all three factor models fit well, although BIC favored the merged model. For school psychologists, a network finding like this one does not settle what an index score means. That question depends on evidence about the scores themselves, such as how reliably index differences can be measured and whether they relate to a child's functioning, which this study did not examine.
